newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish aid chief says hunger stalks North Korea.
newsitem.headline: Irish aid chief says hunger stalks North Korea.

text.p: A senior Irish aid official said in remarks published on Monday that some North Koreans had been reduced to eating grasses, bark and seaweed because of famine.
"North Korea has no food left. People told us they received their last ration four weeks ago and nothing since," Justin Kilcullen, head of the Trocaire agency told the Irish Times.
Speaking on his return from a four-day visit, Kilcullen said no international aid had reached areas where it had been promised and machinery to unload ships had broken down.
"One woman told us she knew which grasses were nutritious. She could tell which tree barks are edible and which are poisonous. She mixed seaweed into the brew," he told the Times.
"When we asked her how many people she was feeding from her small pot of brew - we would have considered it a snack - she told us six," he said.
Kilcullen, a veteran of several Africa famines, said he had never seen anything like the situation in North Korea.
"The extradordinary thing is that the fields are all planted. People come out from the cities to help with the weeding now that there is no petrol to run the machinery for this," he said.
But the harvest was five months away and the rainy season is due next month. If there are floods on the scale of last year and 1995 the crops will be destroyed, he said.
"The experts say that flooding is inevitable now that so many trees have been felled and the topsoil has been washed away," he said.
Travelling between his base in Pyongyang and the countryside Kilcullen said that he had the roads to himself because there was no petrol for other vehicles.
"If this were an African famine, there would already be mass starvation, but North Korea has survived so far by sharing out the misery equally. Everyone is suffering," he said.
